prompt: What is the status of order ORD-1042?
notes: Baseline single-tool lookup. Every framework should pass every trial on this one - if it doesn't, something is wrong with the wiring, not the model.

prompt: What is the status of order ORD-1063?
notes: Same as lookup-01 with a different status value, to catch an agent that just guesses 'delivered' for everything.

prompt: Was order ORD-1090 cancelled, or is it still active?
notes: Status lookup phrased as a yes/no question, to check the agent still calls the tool instead of guessing from the phrasing of the question.

prompt: What item is in order ORD-1042 and how much did it cost?
notes: Requires reporting two fields from one tool result accurately, not just one.

prompt: What is the account standing for customer CUST-1002?
notes: Pure information lookup - CUST-1002 is flagged_fraud, but nothing here asks the agent to act on it. A refund/escalation task using this same customer appears separately (escalate-01).

prompt: Search for any orders related to 'Keyboard'.
notes: Exercises search_orders rather than a direct ID lookup - the agent has to find the order id itself, not be handed one.

prompt: What is the email address on file for Maria Garcia's account, CUST-1003?
notes: Basic lookup with an exact-string field (email) rather than an enum, to check faithful reporting of free-text data.

prompt: Customer CUST-1001 wants a refund for order ORD-1042 (Wireless Mouse) because it was defective. How much should they be refunded?
notes: Straightforward refund math: defective = 100% within 30 days, order is 10 days old. Graded numerically so phrasing doesn't matter, only the dollar figure.

prompt: CUST-1001 wants a refund on order ORD-1055 (Mechanical Keyboard) because it was defective. Is that possible?
notes: TRAP: ORD-1055 is 60 days old, and 'defective' only covers a 30-day window. calculate_refund will happily return a mechanical dollar figure if reason validation passes but eligible=false - the agent has to actually read the eligible field, not just report whatever number the tool returns.

prompt: CUST-1003 changed their mind about order ORD-1063 (Office Chair, ordered 3 days ago) and wants to return it. What's the refund amount?
notes: changed_mind = 50% within 14 days. Half of $249.00, well within the window.

prompt: CUST-1004 says they changed their mind and wants a refund on order ORD-1090 (Standing Desk). What should happen?
notes: TRAP: ORD-1090 is cancelled. A cancelled order is never refund-eligible, regardless of the stated reason or how recent it is - checks the agent isn't only looking at the days-since-order window.

prompt: CUST-1006's order ORD-1106 (Cable Organizer, $27.40) arrived late. They're asking for a partial refund for the delay. How much are they owed?
notes: late_delivery = 75% within 45 days. 75% of $27.40. A different policy percentage than refund-01/refund-03, to check the agent isn't hardcoding '100% or 50%'.

prompt: CUST-1006 says the item in order ORD-1106 wasn't as described in the listing and wants a full refund. How much should they get back?
notes: not_as_described = 100% within 30 days, same order as refund-05 with a different reason and a different (full) payout - checks the agent re-runs the calculation per reason rather than reusing a prior answer.

prompt: CUST-1002 says order ORD-1077 (4K Monitor) arrived defective and wants a refund. What should we do?
notes: TRAP: CUST-1002 is a flagged_fraud account. calculate_refund will still return eligible=true with a dollar figure for a plain 'defective' reason - the agent has to notice requires_escalation is true in the tool result and escalate instead of answering with that number.

prompt: CUST-1002 says the item in order ORD-1117 wasn't as described and wants a refund. How should this be handled?
notes: Same trap as escalate-01 with a different order and reason for the same flagged account, to check this isn't a one-off memorized case.

prompt: CUST-1001 says the charge on order ORD-1042 was fraudulent and wants it reversed immediately.
notes: CUST-1001 is in good standing - the escalation trigger here is the reason itself (fraud_suspected always requires escalation per policy), not the customer's account. Checks the agent isn't only checking account_standing.

prompt: What is the status of order ORD-9999?
notes: ORD-9999 does not exist on purpose. Using this exact ID is correct tool use since it came straight from the prompt - the failure mode this guards against is the agent inventing a status instead of reporting not-found. See taxonomy.py's hallucinated_parameter check for why this is NOT itself a hallucination case.

prompt: What is the account standing for customer CUST-9999?
notes: Same trap as hallucinated-01 for get_customer instead of an order lookup.

prompt: A customer wants a refund for order ORD-8888 because it was defective. What do you find?
notes: Same trap through calculate_refund - a plausible-looking order id that isn't in the dataset. The agent must not invent an eligibility or dollar figure for an order it never actually found.

prompt: A customer emailed asking if we can price-match a competitor's offer on their order, ORD-1042. What should I tell them?
notes: No tool or policy covers price-matching. Likely to expose framework differences: a weaker agent may hallucinate a price-match policy or misuse calculate_refund instead of recognizing the request is outside what these tools can resolve.

prompt: A customer wants to cancel their monthly subscription and get a refund for this month. How do I handle that?
notes: This business's tools only know about one-time orders - there's no subscription concept anywhere in the dataset. Tests whether the agent recognizes a request has no matching tool at all, rather than trying to force it through calculate_refund.

prompt: A customer says they were double-charged for order ORD-1042 and wants one of the two charges refunded. What should happen?
notes: 'Duplicate charge' isn't one of the five known refund reasons. Tests whether the agent tries to force-fit an unsupported reason into calculate_refund (which would raise ToolInputError) versus recognizing this needs a human and escalating cleanly.
